chapters.title: The Word of Blessing
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 1

1The word of blessing of Enoch, with which he blessed the chosen and the righteous, who will be there on the day of distress, when all the evil and the wicked are removed.

2And Enoch answered and said — a righteous man, whose eyes were opened by God, and he saw:

3Concerning the chosen I speak, and concerning them I took up my parable — the Great Holy One will come out from His dwelling,

4and the God of the age will tread upon Mount Sinai, and appear in the strength of His power from heaven.

5And they will fear. And the Watchers will believe, and they will sing hidden things in all the ends of the earth, and all the ends of the earth will shake.

6And the high mountains will be shaken and will fall and be broken apart, and the high hills will be brought low, and they will melt like honeycomb before the flame.

7And the earth will be split with a great chasm, and everything on the earth will be destroyed, and there will be judgment on all.

8And with the righteous He will make peace, and over the chosen there will be protection and peace, and He will help them.

9And here — He came with ten thousands of holy ones, to carry out judgment on them, and to destroy the wicked, and to bring a charge against all flesh for everything that sinners and the wicked have done and committed against Him.

Notes

  • On this book, and a warning about one of its witnesses — 1 Enoch does not survive whole in the language it was written in. The complete text exists only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic); behind it stand fragments of Greek, and behind those, fragments of the Aramaic original from Qumran. This rendering follows the fullest witness at each point and the notes say which one that is. One caution applies throughout: the Ge'ez transcription in this repository is incomplete. Two thirds of its verses break off mid-sentence — they are cut short in our copy, not in the Ethiopic tradition. So where a note below reports what the Ge'ez says, that is evidence. Nothing here argues from what the Ge'ez appears to leave out, because our copy is not in a position to tell us.

  • v1 "when all the evil and the wicked are removed" — the Ge'ez says the evil and the wicked. The Greek says all the enemies — a political word where the Ge'ez has a moral one. The Greek also closes the verse with four words that are not in our Ge'ez line: and the righteous will be saved.

  • v1 "the chosen and the righteous" — the Ge'ez joins them with and, making two groups. The Greek has no and: chosen righteous, one group described twice. Much of this book turns on who the chosen are, and the two witnesses differ in the opening sentence about whether that is one category or two.

  • v3–4 "the Great Holy One will come out from His dwelling" — this half-line is in the Aramaic (the Gr[eat] Holy One will go forth from) and in the Greek. Our Ge'ez line breaks off just before it.

  • v4 "in the strength of His power" — from the Aramaic: he will appear in the [might] of [his] streng[th]. The Ge'ez word at this point is different — ba-te'yentu, in His camp or host, an army rather than a display of force. Three independent readings of the Ge'ez were checked against this: two read it as camp, one as power, and the one that read power gave the Aramaic's word rather than the Ethiopic's. The Greek breaks off here and cannot settle it.

  • v5 "the Watchers" — the Greek has all will be afraid, and the Watchers will believe, and they will sing hidden things in all the ends of the earth, and the Aramaic independently confirms the ending: [al]l the end[s of the earth will tremble]. The Watchers — egrēgoroi, the sleepless ones — are the subject of chapters 6 through 16 and the reason the book exists. This is their first appearance.

  • v6 "melt like honeycomb before the flame" — the image is in the Ge'ez; the Greek breaks off before it. English Enochs traditionally print like wax, which is the smoother phrase, but the Ge'ez word is honeycomb, and three independent readings of it agree.

  • v6 "shaken... fall... broken apart" — the Greek gives the mountains three verbs where the Ge'ez gives one. The single Ge'ez verb is built on a root used for being startled or frightened, so it may carry more than physical shaking, but it is regularly used of things trembling and this verse alone does not settle it.

  • v7 "the earth will be split with a great chasm" — the Greek has the earth split. The Ge'ez verb at this point is wa-tesattam, and it will be submerged — the world ends by water, not by cracking open. This is a genuine difference between the witnesses, and it survives the caution above, because it is a word the Ge'ez has rather than one it lacks. It is also the first thing a fluent paraphrase destroys: of three independent readings of this word, two glossed it submerged and then one of those two silently printed rent asunder in its English.

  • v8 "with the righteous He will make peace" — the Greek says with; the Ge'ez says upon. And where the Ge'ez says righteous twice, the Greek distinguishes: peace with the righteous, protection and peace upon the chosen. If those are two groups, this verse promises them different things.

  • v9 "And here — He came" — this is the verse the New Testament quotes. Jude 14–15 attributes it to Enoch, the seventh from Adam, and quotes it closely: Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads, to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly. Jude's last two words are sinners, ungodly — the same pair in the same order that ends this verse in the Ge'ez. Jude uses a past tense, as does the surviving Latin scrap (Ecce venit), while the Greek witness here has the present, he comes. The Ge'ez verb is the perfect form, grammatically past, but Semitic prophecy regularly states a future event in the perfect as something already done, so the form does not settle the tense.

chapters.title: Observe All the Works in Heaven
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 2

1Observe all the works in heaven, how they do not change their paths — and the lights in heaven, how each one rises and sets, each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals, and they do not overstep their own order.

2Look at the earth, and think carefully about the works that are done on it, from first to last: how none of God's works changes, and all of them appear to you.

3Look at the signs of summer and of winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and the clouds pour out rain over it.

Notes

  • v1 "Observe" — the first word of a sequence running to the end of chapter 5. Four times the reader is told to look at something in nature — the stars, the earth, the trees, the seasons — and each time the point is that they keep to their orders. The argument being built is that people do not.

  • v1 "each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals" — from the Greek. This is not decorative: the whole of 1 Enoch 72–82 is a solar calendar argued against the lunar one, and they appear at their festivals is the opening move. The feast days are set by the lights, and the lights do not drift.

  • v2 "Look at the earth" — the Aramaic from Qumran has a word the Greek does not: Co[ntemplate] the earth and o[bse]rve its works — the earth's own works, rather than God's works upon it.

  • v3 "the signs of summer and of winter" — the word signs is in the Aramaic only. The Ge'ez and Greek both have simply summer and winter; the Aramaic has the signs of each. A sign is something meant to be read. The oldest witness makes the seasons a text; the later two make them weather.

  • v3 "the clouds pour out rain" — the Aramaic is the fullest witness here and the only one that names the clouds pouring. The Ge'ez gives a list — water, and cloud and dew and rain — with no verb at all.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 2

Observe all the works in heaven, how they do not change their paths — and the lights in heaven, how each one rises and sets, each ordered in its appointed time, and they appear at their festivals, and they do not overstep their own order.
Look at the earth, and think carefully about the works that are done on it, from first to last: how none of God's works changes, and all of them appear to you.
Look at the signs of summer and of winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and the clouds pour out rain over it.

chapters.title: The Trees That Do Not Shed
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 3

1Observe and see how all the trees look withered, and all their leaves are stripped off — except fourteen trees, which do not shed, but keep the old leaves for two or three years until the new ones come.

Notes

  • v1 "fourteen trees" — the number is in the Ge'ez. The Aramaic says all the tr[ees], all of them, appear withered, with no exception made for fourteen of them, and the Greek here is a torn line reading only observe and see all the trees. Whether the exception is original or later cannot be decided from what survives.

  • v1 "keep the old leaves for two or three years" — from the Aramaic: [their] lea[ves] remain [... until] two or three [years pass]. A detail about evergreens preserved in a Dead Sea fragment.

  • On the shortest chapter — one verse, and the witnesses do not agree about its content. It is a fair sample of what reading this book is like.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 3

Observe and see how all the trees look withered, and all their leaves are stripped off — except fourteen trees, which do not shed, but keep the old leaves for two or three years until the new ones come.

chapters.title: The Heat of Summer
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 4

1And again observe the days of summer, how the sun is above the earth and right over against it. And you look for shade and shelter from the heat of the sun, and the earth burns with scorching heat, and you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock because of its heat.

Notes

  • v1 — there is no Greek for this chapter. The witnesses are the Ge'ez and a torn Aramaic fragment, and they agree closely: the searching for shade, the inability to walk on ground or rock, the heat. Where two witnesses this far apart in age and language line up phrase by phrase, the wording behind both is likely close to original.

  • v1 "observe the days of summer" — the Aramaic again has the signs of summer, as it did in 2:3, where the Ge'ez has days. The same difference twice in two chapters is a pattern, not a slip: one tradition is reading the seasons as signs to be interpreted, the other as periods of time.

  • v1 "you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock" — the Aramaic reads the du[st] and on its rocks. Dust, not ground. It is the word from Genesis 2:7, the stuff the first man was made of, and the sun makes it untouchable.

speech.text: 1 Enoch 4

And again observe the days of summer, how the sun is above the earth and right over against it. And you look for shade and shelter from the heat of the sun, and the earth burns with scorching heat, and you cannot walk on the ground or on the rock because of its heat.

chapters.title: But You Have Not Held Fast
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 5

1Observe how the trees cover themselves with green leaves, and how all their fruit is for honor and glory. Think carefully about all His works, and understand that the living God made them so, and that He lives for all the ages.

2And all His works stand before Him, going on from year to year in the same way, and all His works carry out their tasks for Him and do not change — everything happens just as it was commanded.

3And see how the sea and the rivers do the same, and do not change their works from His word.

4But you have not held fast, and you have not done according to His commandments. You have turned away, and you have spoken great and hard words with your unclean mouth against His greatness. You have spoken against Him in your lies, you hard-hearted — there is no peace for you.

5And because of this you will curse your days, and the years of your life will be destroyed.

6Then your names will become an everlasting curse to all the righteous, and by you all who curse will curse, and all the sinners and the wicked will swear by you.

7And for the chosen there will be light and favor and peace, and they will inherit the earth. But for you, the wicked, there will be a curse.

8Then light and favor will be given to the chosen, and they will inherit the earth. Then wisdom will be given to all the chosen, and they will all live, and they will never sin again — not through unfaithfulness and not through pride. In the enlightened man there will be light, and in the understanding man, insight, and they will not go wrong.

9And they will not sin all the days of their life, and they will not die in burning anger, but they will complete the number of the days of their life. And their life will grow in peace, and the years of their joy will be multiplied in gladness and in everlasting peace, through all the days of their life.

Notes

  • v1 "for honor and glory" — in the Greek, and, broken, in the Aramaic (for maj]estic splen[dor). The point of the whole nature sequence turns on it: the fruit is not for eating, it is for honor. Obedience is being described as a kind of beauty.

  • v2 "everything happens just as it was commanded" — the Greek and the Aramaic agree on how this sentence ends; the Aramaic independently has all of them perform his word.

  • v4 "you have spoken great and hard words with your unclean mouth" — the charge, and the reason for everything that follows. The Greek and the Aramaic carry it almost phrase for phrase: But you have changed your works [... and have spo]ken against him great and harsh words with the mouth of your impurity; [... hearts,] there will be no peace for you. Where two witnesses this far apart in age and language line up this closely, the wording behind both is likely near the original.

  • v4 "there is no peace for you" — a refrain in this book, and it lands on the accused rather than on their circumstances. Nothing is said about what will happen to them. It is said about what they are.

  • v6 "all the sinners and the wicked will swear by you" — a name used in an oath is a name people trust. The curse is that these names stay in use — as the standard of what a wrecked life looks like.

  • v8 "wisdom will be given to all the chosen" — the most hopeful sentence in the first five chapters, and it survives in the Greek: wisdom, life, the end of sin, light in the enlightened man, insight in the understanding one.

  • v9 "they will complete the number of the days of their life" — the promise is not immortality. It is that the count runs out on time. Against chapter 6, where two hundred beings come down and ruin exactly this, it is the argument of the book stated in advance.

chapters.title: In the Days of Jared
chapters.html:
1 Enoch 6

1And it came to pass, when the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that beautiful daughters were born to them.

2And the angels, the sons of heaven, saw them and desired them, and said to one another, "Come, let us choose wives for ourselves from the sons of men, and let us father children for ourselves."

3And Semyaza, who was their leader, said to them, "I am afraid you will not want this deed done, and I alone will pay the penalty for this great sin."

4And they all answered him and said, "Let us all swear an oath, and bind ourselves to one another under a curse, that we will not turn back from this plan, but will carry this plan out in fact."

5Then they all swore together, and all bound themselves to one another under a curse upon it.

6And they were two hundred in all, and they came down in the days of Jared onto the summit of Mount Hermon.

7And these are the names of their chiefs: Semyaza, who was their leader, Urakibarameel, Akibeel, Tamiel, Ramuel, Danel, Ezeqeel, Saraquyal, Asael, Armaros, Batarael, Ananel, Zaqeel, Samsapeel, Satarel, Turel, Yomyael, Arazyal.

8These are their chiefs — the chiefs of the tens.

Notes

  • v1 "when the sons of men had multiplied... beautiful daughters were born to them" — this is Genesis 6:1 almost word for word: And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them. Genesis gives the episode four verses and moves on to the flood. 1 Enoch gives it ten chapters. Whichever direction the borrowing ran, the two books tell the same story and only one of them explains it.

  • v2 "the angels, the sons of heaven" — Genesis 6:2 calls them bene ha-Elohim, the sons of God, and says nothing more about who they are. This book calls them angels in its second sentence on the subject and never treats the question as open.

  • v3 "I alone will pay the penalty" — the leader's objection is not that the plan is wrong. It is that he will be left holding it. The oath in the next verse is his fix: make everyone equally guilty. The book's account of how a group does something none of them would do alone is four verses long and has not dated.

  • v6 "in the days of Jared" — the Greek and the Aramaic both date the descent this way (in the days of Jared up[on...). At this point the Ge'ez instead names a place, Ardis, which appears nowhere else — three independent readings of the Ge'ez agree on the word. Our Ethiopic line then breaks off mid-clause at which is, so whether it went on to name Jared or Hermon cannot be told from our copy.

  • v6 "Jared" — in Genesis 5:18 Jared is Enoch's father. The name in Hebrew is Yered, from the verb yarad, to come down. The Watchers come down in the days of Descent. The Aramaic has the same consonants for the name and for the act, which makes this one of the few wordplays in the book checkable in an original language rather than through a translation.

  • v6 "Mount Hermon" — the name is in the Greek (Hermoniem); the Aramaic fragment breaks off just before it. In Hebrew, cherem is the word for something placed under a ban or a binding curse — which is what the two hundred have just done to each other in vv4–5. No surviving witness connects the two. The mountain and the oath simply carry the same sound, one verse apart.

  • v7 "Urakibarameel" — the list has eighteen names. The next verse calls these the chiefs of the tens, and two hundred split into tens needs twenty. This name looks like two run together, which would make nineteen. The count in the text we have does not reach the number the text itself gives.

  • v8 "the chiefs of the tens" — the Aramaic is the fullest witness: These are the chiefs, and the chief[s] of the ten[s] — two ranks, not one. The Greek has one rank; our Ge'ez line breaks off at These are.
